meta.regime: Two correlated shocks still run against each other on this board - the Middle East energy premium, which is inflationary, and the AI capital-spending repricing, which is not - and the first dated resolution of the week has now landed in a way that splits them. The US midterms delivered a Democratic Senate, the market read that as removing a deficit-expanding agenda, real yields fell and the dollar is the weakest currency here: gold is back at 3999.83 and silver plus 3.01%, but copper is minus 0.24% and at its lowest since August 19, so the real-rate leg has reversed while the demand leg has not.

US and Canadian payrolls then print together Friday at 13:30Z, Ueda speaks Friday 16:00Z and New Zealand votes Saturday.

dailyRead: The first of this week's four binaries has resolved, and the way it resolved matters more than the result. Democrats took the US Senate - the Associated Press called it late Tuesday, Forbes described a decisive rout, and while CBS reports both chambers the House call is not uniformly confirmed, so treat the Senate as settled and the House as probable. The market's reading was not about who won but about what a split Congress removes: the odds of a deficit-expanding agenda over the next two years. Treasuries rallied, both nominal and real yields fell, and the dollar is the weakest currency on this board - DXY is 101.435 and minus 0.45%, minus 0.74% on the week. Every major gained against it: EUR/USD 1.12390 and plus 0.42%, GBP/USD 1.34640 and plus 0.37%, NZD/USD 0.56055 and plus 0.37%, AUD/USD 0.69851 and plus 0.27%, USD/CHF 0.81672 and minus 0.50%, USD/JPY 157.998 and minus 0.43%, USD/CAD 1.39611 and minus 0.35%. Now the part that is the trade, because it is the thing that did not happen. Yesterday this file led with the AI-capital-spending crack draining the hike premium out of the board, and the evidence was gold at its worst month since 2008, silver minus 19.29% and copper falling. Today gold is 3999.83 and plus 1.73%, silver 51.293 and plus 3.01% - the two biggest single-day gains on the commodity board - and copper is 6.3634 and minus 0.24%, minus 4.25% on the week, at its lowest since August 19 on the LME. That divergence is diagnostic. Gold and silver rose because US real yields fell on an election result; copper did not rise because nothing changed about AI demand. So the monetary leg of the AI shock has reversed and the demand leg has not, and that splits this board rather than lifting it. It helps the havens and gold. It does nothing for the three currencies whose own central banks named AI demand as a reason to tighten - the RBA cited AI-related demand for technology goods on Monday, Ueda cited strong global AI demand on October 30, and the RBNZ's October minutes attributed part of the rise in global yields to AI capital demand. December Fed pricing is roughly where it was: CME FedWatch 71.4%, Polymarket 72.5% and Kalshi 73%, against about 80% a week ago, so the election did not rebuild it. Second, and the clearest score change on the board, the franc. Swiss October CPI came in at 1.5% year over year against a 1.3% consensus and 1.0% in September, the highest since 2023, with the index at 101.7 and prices plus 0.2% on the month. The composition is the whole story: energy accounted for about 96% of the net monthly increase and CPI excluding petroleum products was unchanged on the month, while core held at 0.5%. So this is the Hormuz shock arriving in Swiss headline inflation rather than a Swiss inflation problem - which is exactly why it is tradeable. The franc was already the one haven that worked through the equity correction, and today it is the strongest currency on this board outright, gaining against all seven others: USD/CHF minus 0.50% and minus 1.66% on the month, EUR/CHF 0.91784 and minus 1.53% on the month, AUD/CHF minus 0.21% and minus 2.31% on the week, NZD/CHF minus 1.70% on the week. The franc goes to plus two and takes joint top of the board. The cap is unchanged and explicit - the SNB is at 0.00%, core at 0.5% lets it hold on December 10, and it has repeated it will intervene in FX as necessary - but TradingEconomics carries 0.25% in Q1/27, and a print above consensus with the energy pass-through still in the pipeline makes that date more real than it was yesterday. Third, Canada, where the words changed. Macklem told the House of Commons Standing Committee on Finance on Tuesday that further rate hikes may be needed, with decisions taken meeting by meeting, and put CPI at 3.5% by year-end, at or above 3% through much of 2027 and back near 2% only by mid-2028. He attributed the pickup to the Middle East energy shock rather than domestic demand and said federal spending is not really driving inflation. That is a materially firmer line than the no-predetermined-path framing this file carried yesterday, and it moves December 9 from a coin flip toward a lean. The counterweight is in the same testimony: the economy still runs with spare capacity, which is what complicates further tightening. USD/CAD is minus 2.10% on the month. Friday's employment print at 13:30Z against a plus 14.6k forecast, after September's minus 68,300, is the swing input, and the federal budget lands November 5. Fourth, sterling, which still keeps the board outright but is now priced. Tomorrow at 12:00Z the MPC is 93.5% to 94% to take Bank Rate to 4.00%, ForexFactory carries a 7-0-2 vote forecast against September's 3-0-6 hold, Goldman expects 7-2 and Oxford Economics sees November and February together taking the rate to 4.25%. The data supports it - CPI 3.5% with core 2.8%, unemployment down to 4.7%, employment plus 102,000 and wage growth 3.7% - and GBP/USD is plus 1.83% on the month. The honest caveat is that at 94% there is far more room for disappointment than for confirmation, and the disappointment has a name and a time: a Monetary Policy Report that caps the path at 4.00%, and Bailey at 12:30Z. Fifth, the yen, which finally took a haven bid - but only against the dollar. USD/JPY is minus 0.43% and FXStreet describes the pair recovering from a three-week low as softer US yields met intervention risk. On the crosses the move barely exists: EUR/JPY minus 0.06%, GBP/JPY minus 0.09%, CHF/JPY plus 0.04%, NZD/JPY minus 0.08%. USD/JPY is plus 0.06% on the month, which is to say nowhere. So today was a dollar event rather than yen demand, the December 18 hike stays 75% to 80% priced with Takata already dissenting for an immediate 1.5%, and the pair is still held by Katayama's warning that the joint FX statement stands - 159.00 is the zone where the Ministry of Finance has acted before. Express the yen against the franc, not against the dollar. Sixth, oil, which has stalled harder than it looked. WTI is 96.331 and plus 0.25%, Brent 103.955 and plus 0.34%, but the week is minus 6.28% and minus 6.88% - the premium has come out without a deal. The diplomacy is genuinely contradictory: Araghchi says Tehran's conditions are feasible if Washington shows goodwill and that Qatari mediation compressed the plan to two days, Qatar is working on the release of more than $6 billion in Iranian assets, and Trump wrote that a deal could happen while also threatening the hammer - yet the Wall Street Journal reports the main diplomatic channel has stalled, there were fresh US strikes on the eve of the elections, and Iran has played down hopes of ending the war. Both tails stay live inside the same week and the physical constraint has not changed. Finally the two currencies that lost ground. Australia goes from plus one to zero, and the specific leg that broke is nameable: the RBA hiked to 4.85% on Monday citing AI-related demand for technology goods, and copper - the cleanest market read on that demand - refused the day's metals rally and sits at its lowest since August 19. AUD/USD rose only 0.27% on a day the dollar fell 0.45%, it is minus 0.97% on the week, and it fell against the franc, the yen and the Canadian dollar. Bullock has given no guidance, December 8 reads as a hold, and the minutes on November 17 are the next read. New Zealand stays at minus two: the kiwi gained 0.37% against a falling dollar and lost ground on every cross that matters - EUR/NZD 2.00450 and plus 0.55%, GBP/NZD 2.40161 and plus 0.50%, AUD/NZD 1.24613 and plus 0.38%. After Monday's labour miss the December 9 call is genuinely split - UOB and Westpac still expect 3.00%, ActionForex calls a hike more likely than not, Moody's argues weak wages back another hold - and no verified post-print market probability is available, so front-end swaps rather than spot are the thing to watch into Saturday's election.

today.headline: October CPI jumped to 1.5% against a 1.3% forecast, a three-year high, and the franc gained against all seven other currencies.
today.read: The print is the day's cleanest new fact and the composition makes it tradeable rather than alarming. Headline CPI is 1.5% year over year from 1.0%, above the 1.3% consensus and the highest since 2023, with the index at 101.7 and prices plus 0.2% on the month - but energy accounted for roughly 96% of the net monthly increase, CPI excluding petroleum products was unchanged, and core held at 0.5%. So this is the Hormuz energy shock arriving in Swiss headline inflation, not a domestic inflation problem, which is why it does not force the SNB and does strengthen the currency. The franc was already the one haven that worked through the Nasdaq correction and the gold liquidation; today it was strongest outright: USD/CHF 0.81672 and minus 0.50%, minus 1.66% on the month, EUR/CHF 0.91784 and minus 0.09%, minus 1.53% on the month, GBP/CHF minus 0.12%, AUD/CHF minus 0.21% and minus 2.31% on the week, NZD/CHF minus 0.12% and minus 1.70% on the week, CAD/CHF minus 0.16%, CHF/JPY 193.404 and plus 0.04%, plus 1.72% on the month. The score goes to plus two and the franc takes joint top of this board. The ceiling is still policy and still explicit - core at 0.5% lets the SNB hold on December 10, 1.5% is inside the 0% to 2% band, and the Bank has repeated it will intervene in FX as necessary - but TradingEconomics carries 0.25% in Q1/27 and today made that date more credible. Invalidation would be a Hormuz settlement that reverses the energy pass-through alongside an AI-capex recovery, which would remove the inflation leg and the haven bid together.

today.headline: Democrats took the Senate, the market priced out a deficit-expanding agenda, real yields fell and the dollar is the weakest currency on the board at minus 0.45%.
today.read: The first of the week's four binaries resolved close to the base case this file carried - a Democratic sweep was 74% to 78% on Kalshi and Polymarket - but the reaction was larger than priced-in should imply, and the channel is fiscal rather than monetary. The Associated Press called the Senate late Tuesday, Forbes described a decisive rout, and CBS reports both chambers although the House call is not uniformly confirmed, so the Senate is settled and the House probable. Markets read a split Congress as removing the odds of further deficit expansion over the next two years: Treasuries rallied, both nominal and real yields fell, and Pepperstone's Chris Weston tied gold's strength directly to a weaker dollar and a punchy decline in nominal and real yields. DXY is 101.435 and minus 0.45%, minus 0.74% on the week and minus 0.72% on the month. Every major gained: EUR/USD plus 0.42%, GBP/USD plus 0.37%, NZD/USD plus 0.37%, AUD/USD plus 0.27%, USD/CHF minus 0.50%, USD/JPY minus 0.43%, USD/CAD minus 0.35%. The score stays at zero rather than going negative, because the monetary case did not change: the data is still the hottest here at 3.7% CPI and 6.3% PPI, two FOMC members voted to hike in October, and December pricing is essentially unmoved at 71.4% on CME FedWatch, 72.5% on Polymarket and 73% on Kalshi against about 80% a week ago. The election removed a dollar-supportive fiscal leg without touching the rate leg. Friday's payrolls at 13:30Z against a plus 65k forecast, after September's plus 29k, is what resolves the rate leg, and a strong print rebuilds December and the dollar with it.

today.headline: Macklem told the Commons finance committee that further rate hikes may be needed and put CPI at 3.5% by year-end, which moves December 9 from a coin flip to a lean.
today.read: This is a change in the words rather than the data, and it is the kind that reprices a meeting. Appearing before the House of Commons Standing Committee on Finance on November 3, Macklem said further rate hikes may be needed with decisions taken meeting by meeting, forecast CPI reaching 3.5% by year-end, staying at or above 3% through much of 2027 and returning close to the 2% target only by mid-2028, and attributed the pickup mainly to the Middle East energy shock rather than excess domestic demand. He also said federal spending is not really driving inflation and that he does not see fiscal policy working against the Bank. Set against the October 28 framing of no predetermined path, that is a firmer line, and it arrives with the Bank already having delivered its first hike in three years to 2.50%. The honest counterweight is in the same testimony: Canada still operates with spare capacity, which is precisely what complicates further tightening, and analysts picked that up as the limiting factor. USD/CAD is 1.39611 and minus 0.35%, minus 2.10% on the month, so the currency continues to follow the terms-of-trade improvement this file flagged two days ago - but crude is minus 6.28% on the week, which cuts the other way. The score holds at plus one with a firmer forward lean. Two dated inputs: the federal budget on November 5, and Friday's employment print at 13:30Z against a plus 14.6k forecast after September's minus 68,300 - the same minute as US payrolls.

today.headline: Copper refused the day's metals rally and sits at its lowest since August 19, which breaks the AI-demand leg the RBA built Monday's hike on - the score goes to zero.
today.read: This is a specific leg failing rather than a drift, and it is worth naming precisely. On Monday the RBA hiked to 4.85% on a 6-3 vote and the statement cited elevated fuel and commodity prices, tighter domestic capacity and AI-related demand for technology goods as the sources of broad-based price pressure. Copper is the cleanest market read on that last item, and on a day when gold rose 1.73% and silver rose 3.01% on falling US real yields, copper went the other way: 6.3634 and minus 0.24%, minus 4.25% on the week, minus 3.37% on the month and at its lowest since August 19 on the LME. Reuters-tracked base metals fell on a renewed selloff in Asian technology stocks, and BMO notes AI investment is one of the few engines of industrial growth while construction and autos stay sluggish. So the monetary leg of the AI shock reversed today and the demand leg did not, and Australia is on the wrong side of that split. The price action agrees. AUD/USD is 0.69851 and plus 0.27% on a day the dollar fell 0.45%, which is underperformance, and it is minus 0.97% on the week; the currency fell against the franc at minus 0.21%, the yen at minus 0.16% and the Canadian dollar at minus 0.06%, and lost to both the euro and sterling. Australia still holds the highest policy rate on this board at 4.85%, which is what keeps the score at zero rather than negative, but it now has no forward guidance, a domestic labour market that shed 39,300 jobs in September with unemployment at 4.7% and rising, and a commodity complex questioning its inflation case. December 8 is a hold, February is the meeting to trade, and the minutes on November 17 are the next real read. A copper recovery restores this quickly.

today.headline: The yen finally took a haven bid, recovering from a three-week low as US real yields fell - but it happened only against the dollar, not on the crosses.
today.read: For three sessions this file has noted the yen declining haven bids it should have taken. Today it took one, and the qualification matters more than the fact. USD/JPY is 157.998 and minus 0.43%, which FXStreet attributes to softer US yields meeting live intervention risk. But look across the board: EUR/JPY 177.511 and minus 0.06%, GBP/JPY 212.685 and minus 0.09%, CHF/JPY 193.404 and plus 0.04%, AUD/JPY 110.368 and minus 0.16%, NZD/JPY 88.552 and minus 0.08%, CAD/JPY 113.138 and minus 0.11%. Those are rounding errors. The pair is plus 0.06% on the month and plus 0.10% on the week, which is to say the yen has gone nowhere; what moved today was the dollar. The forward case is unchanged and remains the strongest part of the story: the October 30 hold was 8-1 with Takata dissenting for an immediate move to 1.5%, the Bank lifted FY2027 inflation to 2.6% from 2.4%, Ueda told parliament underlying inflation is quite close to 2% and that failing to adjust could stoke an overshoot, swaps imply 75% to 80% for December 18 and TradingEconomics forecasts 1.50%. Two honest caveats. Commentary on the October meeting is split, with some desks reading it as less hawkish than expected. And Ueda's own hawkish reasoning leaned on strong global AI demand, which is the demand copper says is still being repriced. The score holds at plus one. What caps the pair is Katayama's warning that the joint FX statement with the United States stands and that Tokyo will act against disorderly weakness; 159.00 is the zone where the Ministry of Finance has moved before and 160 the line analysts flag, while a break below 156.72 would open 156.00. Ueda speaks Friday at 16:00Z. Express this against the franc rather than the dollar.

today.headline: The kiwi rose 0.37% against a falling dollar and still lost ground on every cross that matters, with EUR/NZD up 0.55% through 2.0045.
today.read: A currency that gains against a dollar falling 0.45% has not gained, and the crosses say so plainly: EUR/NZD 2.00450 and plus 0.55%, GBP/NZD 2.40161 and plus 0.50%, AUD/NZD 1.24613 and plus 0.38%, NZD/CAD 0.78264 and plus 0.02%, NZD/CHF 0.45786 and minus 0.12%. Those were the three largest cross moves on the board today and all three went against the kiwi. NZD/USD is 0.56055, minus 0.35% on the week and minus 2.61% year to date. Monday's Q3 labour data remains the reason and it has not improved on reflection: unemployment 5.7% against a 5.5% forecast and the highest since 2016, employment minus 0.1% on the quarter against plus 0.4%, Q2 revised down to plus 0.3%, participation 70.4% from 70.6% and private-sector wages ex overtime 2.0% year over year against 3.7% inflation. The score holds at minus two. December 9 is now a genuine split rather than a base case: UOB expects 3.00% and Westpac still forecasts a hike, ActionForex calls a move more likely than not, and the RBNZ's own Q4 inflation forecast of 4.4% on fuel pass-through supports them - while Moody's argues weak wages and falling real incomes back another hold, and the NZX 50 rose on the view that the jobs data eased December hike risk. No verified post-print market probability exists, so front-end swaps rather than spot are the thing to watch. Two dated items remain: Saturday's election, where Labour has pledged to restore the dual employment mandate but Westpac notes December 9 proceeds under the current single mandate regardless, and the Financial Stability Report on November 10.

today.headline: EUR/USD rose 0.42% to 1.12390 but nothing euro-specific changed, and the October flash HICP is still to land today.
today.read: The move is a dollar move: the euro was essentially flat against everything else, with EUR/JPY minus 0.06%, EUR/GBP plus 0.03%, EUR/CHF minus 0.09% and EUR/CAD plus 0.05%. EUR/USD is only plus 0.14% on the month, which is the honest measure of how little the euro has actually done. Today's October flash HICP is the near-dated test and it is not yet published: consensus sits at 4.0% and the TradingEconomics forecast at 3.9%, against September's 3.8% - the highest since September 2023, where energy ran at 18.9% from 14.3% and core was 2.5%. A 4-handle would harden a December 17 hike that already prices between 82% and 94% after Lagarde confirmed the Governing Council discussed hiking before holding unanimously. The counterweight is unchanged and sits in the ECB's own statement: energy can fuel inflation while weighing on activity, underlying inflation is broadly stable and negotiated wages are just 2.44%. For the euro area the energy shock is gas rather than crude, and it is still worsening as a growth tax - EU gas is 93.19 EUR/MWh and plus 26.76% on the month, German gas 98.31 and plus 32.00%, even as Brent fell 6.88% on the week. The score holds at plus one. France's fiscal position remains the spread risk the ECB cannot price away.

today.headline: Sterling was quiet into tomorrow's decision, with GBP/USD plus 0.37% on the dollar move and EUR/GBP unchanged at plus 0.03%.
today.read: Nothing moved today because everything is waiting for 12:00Z tomorrow. GBP/USD is 1.34640 and plus 1.83% on the month, GBP/CHF minus 0.12%, GBP/JPY minus 0.09%, GBP/CAD plus 0.03% - and the two big gains, GBP/NZD plus 0.50% and GBP/AUD plus 0.08%, are stories about the kiwi and the Australian dollar rather than about sterling. The setup is as good as a scheduled event gets on the fundamentals and as poor as one gets on the pricing. For it: 93.5% to 94% priced for 4.00%, a ForexFactory 7-0-2 vote forecast against September's 3-0-6 hold, Goldman at 7-2, Nomura seeing the split simply invert, CPI 3.5% with core 2.8%, unemployment down to 4.7%, employment plus 102,000 and wage growth 3.7%, and Oxford Economics expecting November and February together to deliver 4.25%. Against it: at 94% the hike itself is worth almost nothing, so the tradeable risk is one-sided. The Monetary Policy Report lands the same minute as the decision and Reuters has flagged the Bank may use it to push back on bets for several more increases; Bailey follows at 12:30Z. The score holds at plus two into the event and the invalidation is dated to the minute: a Report that caps the path at 4.00% takes sterling off the top of this board.

USD.when: December 9, with new Economic Projections and no November meeting
USD.note: Held at a 4.00% upper bound on October 28 by a 10-2 vote, with both dissenters preferring a hike, and Chair Warsh declined to commit to December. TradingEconomics forecasts 4.25% in Q4/26. EUR.when: December 17, the final 2026 meeting on the ECB calendar
EUR.note: Deposit facility held at 2.50% on October 29 with the refi rate at 2.65%, and Lagarde confirmed at the press conference that the Governing Council discussed a hike before agreeing unanimously to hold. The statement warned elevated energy prices could fuel inflation while weighing on activity, but said underlying inflation is broadly stable with no significant wage response so far - negotiated wage growth is 2.44%. Trackers price December between 82% and 94%. September HICP was 3.8%, the highest since September 2023, with energy at 18.9% against 14.3%, and core 2.5%. JPY.when: December 18, with Ueda speaking Friday November 6 at 16:00Z before then
JPY.note: Held at 1.25% on October 30 by an 8-1 vote, Takata dissenting for an immediate move to 1.5%, after consecutive 25bp hikes in June and September took the rate to its highest since April 1995. The quarterly outlook kept FY2026 inflation at 2.5% and lifted FY2027 to 2.6% from 2.4%. Ueda told parliament underlying inflation is quite close to 2% and that failing to adjust could stoke an overshoot. Swaps imply 75% to 80% for December and TradingEconomics forecasts 1.50%, but commentary is genuinely split - some desks read the October meeting as less hawkish than expected. AUD.when: December 8 at 03:30Z, with the minutes November 17
AUD.note: Hiked 25bp to 4.85% on November 3 on a 6-3 majority, three members preferring a hold, the fifth increase this year and the highest cash rate since late 2008. The statement cited elevated fuel and commodity prices, tighter domestic capacity and AI-related demand for technology goods, and sees inflation above 3% over the coming year. Bullock then gave no forward guidance at all. The AI demand leg is the problem: copper refused today's metals rally, is minus 4.25% on the week and sits at its lowest since August 19, so the commodity most tied to Australia is questioning the reasoning the Board just acted on. December reads as a pause into February.

NZD.when: December 9, with a full Monetary Policy Statement - genuinely two-sided

Q3 labour data on November 3 missed on every measure: unemployment 5.7% against a 5.5% forecast and the highest since 2016, employment minus 0.1% on the quarter against plus 0.4%, Q2 revised down to plus 0.3%, participation 70.4% from 70.6% and private wages 2.0% year over year. For the hike: the October 28 hold was 4-3 with members agreeing further tightening would likely be needed, Governor Breman said afterwards the chance of a December move is high, the RBNZ forecasts 4.4% inflation in December on fuel pass-through, UOB expects 3.00% on December 9 and Westpac still forecasts a hike. CAD.when: December 9 - upgraded from a coin flip to a lean after Macklem's testimony
CAD.note: Hiked 25bp to 2.50% on October 28, the first increase in three years. Macklem then told the House of Commons Standing Committee on Finance on November 3 that further rate hikes may be needed, with decisions meeting by meeting, and put CPI at 3.5% by year-end, at or above 3% through much of 2027 and back near 2% only by mid-2028. He attributed the pickup to the Middle East energy shock rather than domestic demand and said federal spending is not really driving inflation. That is firmer than the no-predetermined-path line he used in October. The counterweight is in the same testimony: the economy still runs with spare capacity. The federal budget lands November 5 and Friday's employment print at a plus 14.6k forecast is the swing input.

CHF.when: December 10, with the Quarterly Bulletin December 16
CHF.note: Held at 0.00% on September 24, unchanged since mid-2025, with the SNB saying the stance remains appropriate and repeating it is willing to intervene in foreign exchange markets as necessary. October CPI then came in at 1.5% year over year against a 1.3% consensus and 1.0% in September, the highest since 2023 - but energy was about 96% of the net monthly increase, CPI excluding petroleum products was unchanged on the month and core held at 0.5%, so December 10 is still a hold and 1.5% remains inside the 0% to 2% band. What the print does change is the Q1 question: the SNB itself forecast a further rise in the fourth quarter, the pass-through is not finished, and TradingEconomics carries 0.25% in Q1/27 then 0.75% by Q3/27.

Today it was strongest outright, gaining against all seven others, and it now also carries an upside inflation surprise that no other currency here got. Read the composition honestly: energy was about 96% of the net monthly increase, CPI ex petroleum products was flat and core held at 0.5%, so this does not force the SNB and December 10 is still a hold inside the 0% to 2% band. The cap is the Bank's standing readiness to intervene in FX. Invalidation is a Hormuz settlement and an AI-capex recovery together, which would take the inflation leg and the haven bid at once.

A copper recovery restores the hawkish leg quickly, and that is the thing to watch rather than the domestic data.

The committee's hawkish wing is intact, two members voted to hike in October, and the inflation data is still the hottest on this board. So a dollar-supportive fiscal leg was removed while the rate leg was left alone. Friday's payrolls at 13:30Z against a plus 65k forecast, after September's plus 29k, is the one dated event that can rebuild December and the dollar together; a soft print with 4.2% unemployment does the opposite and this goes to minus one.

catalysts.event: Australia: RBA Cash Rate, Rate Statement and Monetary Policy Statement (red folder)
catalysts.note: Released. Hiked 25 basis points to 4.85% from 4.60%, in line with the forecast, on a 6-3 majority - the fifth increase this year and the highest cash rate since late 2008. The statement cited elevated fuel and commodity prices, tighter domestic capacity and AI-related demand for technology goods, and sees inflation above 3% over the coming year. That last leg is now the problem: copper refused today's metals rally and sits at its lowest since August 19.

catalysts.event: Australia: RBA Press Conference with Governor Bullock (red folder)
catalysts.note: Released. Bullock declined to provide forward guidance and did not replace the tightening bias the statement dropped, which reads as a pause into February rather than a continuing cycle. AUD/USD is 0.69851 and managed only plus 0.27% on a day the dollar fell 0.45%.

catalysts.event: United States: Congressional Elections (red folder)
catalysts.note: Resolved. The Associated Press called the Senate for Democrats late Tuesday, with Forbes describing a decisive rout and flips reported in Ohio and North Carolina; CBS reports Democrats took both chambers but the House call is not uniformly confirmed, so treat the Senate as settled and the House as probable. The base case had hardened to 74% to 78% on Kalshi and Polymarket. The market traded it as removing a deficit-expanding agenda: Treasuries rallied, nominal and real yields fell, DXY is minus 0.45% and gold is back at 3999.83. December Fed pricing did not move - 71.4% on CME FedWatch.

catalysts.event: New Zealand: Q3 Employment Change and Unemployment Rate (red folder)
catalysts.note: Released and missed on every measure, TradingEconomics-verified. Unemployment 5.7% against a 5.5% forecast and 5.6% previously, the highest since 2016; employment minus 0.1% on the quarter against a plus 0.4% forecast, with Q2 revised down to plus 0.3% from plus 0.5%. Participation fell to 70.4% from 70.6% and private-sector wages ex overtime slowed to 2.0% year over year, so unemployment rose even as people left the workforce. December 9 has gone from base case to genuine split: UOB and Westpac still forecast a hike, Moody's argues for a hold, and no verified post-print pricing exists.

catalysts.event: Euro area: October flash HICP
catalysts.note: Today's near-dated test of a December 17 ECB hike priced between 82% and 94%, and not yet published at the time of this report. Consensus is 4.0% and the TradingEconomics forecast 3.9%, against September's 3.8% - the highest since September 2023, where energy ran at 18.9% from 14.3% and core was 2.5%. A 4-handle hardens December; a miss takes the euro back toward the middle of this board.

catalysts.event: United Kingdom: BoE Official Bank Rate, MPC Vote, Monetary Policy Summary and Monetary Policy Report (red folder)
catalysts.note: The single biggest scheduled event on this board. Forecast 4.00% from 3.75%, priced 93.5% to 94%, with ForexFactory carrying a 7-0-2 vote forecast against September's 3-0-6 hold - a swing of four members - and Goldman expecting 7-2. The Report is the risk rather than the rate: Reuters has flagged the Bank may use it to push back on bets for several more increases. Oxford Economics expects November and February together to deliver 4.25%.

catalysts.event: United Kingdom: BoE Governor Bailey speaks (red folder)
catalysts.note: Thirty minutes after the decision and the second half of the same trade. The question is whether he endorses the path to 4.25% from Q1/27 or caps guidance at 4.00%. With the hike itself 94% priced, this is where the tradeable move actually sits. A capped path takes sterling off the top of this board.

catalysts.event: Canada: Federal Budget
catalysts.note: Lands the day after Macklem told the Commons finance committee that further rate hikes may be needed and that he does not see fiscal policy working against the Bank, saying federal spending is not really driving inflation. Reported by Global News as a November 5 release. Any material loosening would test that assessment directly five weeks before the December 9 decision.

catalysts.event: United States: Non-Farm Employment Change, Unemployment Rate and Average Hourly Earnings (red folder)
catalysts.note: Payrolls forecast at plus 65k from plus 29k, unemployment forecast unchanged at 4.2%, average hourly earnings forecast plus 0.3% from plus 0.1%. This is the data that rebuilds or breaks a December 9 hike priced at 71.4% on CME FedWatch, 72.5% on Polymarket and 73% on Kalshi, down from about 80% a week ago. It is also the only event this week that can reverse the dollar's election-driven decline.

catalysts.event: Canada: Employment Change and Unemployment Rate (red folder)
catalysts.note: Employment forecast at plus 14.6k after September's minus 68,300, unemployment forecast unchanged at 6.5%. Prints the same minute as US payrolls, and is the single biggest input into a December 9 Bank of Canada decision that Macklem's testimony has just moved from a coin flip toward a lean.

catalysts.event: Japan: BoJ Governor Ueda speaks (red folder)
catalysts.note: The last scheduled Ueda appearance before December 18, which swaps price at 75% to 80%. He told parliament on October 30 that underlying inflation is quite close to 2% and that failing to adjust could stoke an overshoot - but he also named strong global AI demand as a source of price pressure, and copper at its lowest since August 19 says that demand is still being repriced. Commentary on the October meeting is split on how hawkish it actually was.

catalysts.note: Labour has pledged to restore the RBNZ's dual employment mandate if elected. Westpac notes the December 9 meeting proceeds under the current single mandate whatever the result, so this is a February-and-beyond institutional risk rather than a December one - which narrows the discount without removing it. The last scheduled repair point for the weakest currency on this board.

catalysts.event: New Zealand: RBNZ Financial Stability Report
catalysts.note: Lands two days after the election and a month before the December decision. With December 9 now a genuine split after the Q3 labour miss, any commentary on the mandate question or on the housing and rates outlook carries more weight than a Financial Stability Report normally would.

catalysts.event: Australia: RBA Meeting Minutes
catalysts.note: The first detailed read on the 6-3 split behind the November 3 hike and on how hard the three dissenters argued the downside. The specific question is how much weight the Board put on AI-related technology demand, since copper has now refused a broad metals rally and sits at its lowest since August 19.

catalysts.event: United States: FOMC Minutes
catalysts.note: The record of the October 28 meeting where two policymakers dissented for a hike and Chair Warsh declined to commit to December. The hawkish wing's reasoning matters more than usual now that pricing sits near 71% to 73% while CPI runs at 3.7% and PPI at 6.3%.

catalysts.event: United States: Fed Beige Book
catalysts.note: Regional anecdote on whether the AI capital-spending slowdown is showing up in real activity, two weeks before the December 9 decision. BMO's point that AI investment is one of the few engines of industrial growth while construction and autos stay sluggish is the thing to test here.

catalysts.event: Euro area: ECB Monetary Policy Meeting Accounts
catalysts.note: The account of the October 29 meeting, where Lagarde confirmed the Governing Council discussed a hike before agreeing unanimously to hold. How close that discussion came is the best available read on December 17, which prices between 82% and 94%.

catalysts.event: United States: FOMC decision with Summary of Economic Projections
catalysts.note: The dot plot meeting, and the resolution of a hike priced at 71% to 73%. There is no November FOMC, so Friday's payrolls and the November CPI are the only major inputs between now and then.

catalysts.note: TradingEconomics forecasts 3.00% from 2.75% and UOB agrees, while Moody's argues weak wages and falling real incomes back another hold. Proceeds under the current single mandate whatever Saturday's election delivers, per Westpac.

catalysts.note: No longer a coin flip. Macklem told the Commons finance committee on November 3 that further rate hikes may be needed, with decisions meeting by meeting, and put CPI at 3.5% by year-end and at or above 3% through much of 2027. Spare capacity is the counterweight he named himself. Friday's employment print is the swing input.

catalysts.note: Still a hold at 0.00%, unchanged since mid-2025, despite October CPI surprising at 1.5% against a 1.3% forecast - core held at 0.5%, energy was about 96% of the net monthly rise and 1.5% remains inside the 0% to 2% band. The TradingEconomics path has 0.25% from Q1/27, and today's print made that date more credible.

catalysts.note: Priced between 82% and 94% for a 25bp move taking the deposit facility to 2.75%. Lagarde confirmed the Council discussed hiking in October before holding unanimously. Today's October flash HICP at a 4.0% consensus is the first real input.

catalysts.event: Iran, the United States and the Strait of Hormuz
catalysts.note: Genuinely contradictory and therefore a two-sided binary. Araghchi says Tehran's conditions are feasible if Washington shows goodwill and that Qatari mediation compressed the plan to two days - US measures on day one, the Strait reopening on day two - with Qatar working on the release of more than $6 billion in Iranian assets. Trump wrote that a deal could happen while also threatening the hammer. Against that: the Wall Street Journal reports the main diplomatic channel has stalled, fresh US strikes landed on the eve of the elections, and Iran has played down hopes of ending the war. The premium has come out of crude anyway - WTI minus 6.28% on the week - without the physical constraint changing.

catalysts.event: The AI capital-spending repricing, and the split that opened today
catalysts.note: The Nasdaq 100 closed November 2 at 27,989.82, 10.4% below its October 6 high in its third correction of 2026, on doubts about AI capex returns and the debt funding it; it is still plus 11% for the year. Today the shock split in two. Its monetary leg reversed - real yields fell on the election and gold rose 1.73% with silver plus 3.01% - while its demand leg did not: copper fell to its lowest since August 19 and is minus 4.25% on the week. Three of these eight central banks cited AI demand as a reason to tighten, so the leg that did not recover is the one that matters for the AUD, NZD and JPY cases.

catalysts.event: Japanese FX intervention risk
catalysts.note: Finance Minister Katayama has said the joint FX statement with the United States still stands and that Tokyo is prepared to act against excessive or disorderly yen weakness. The zone that matters is 159.00, where the Ministry of Finance has acted before, with 160 flagged as the key line; a break below 156.72 would open 156.00. It is what has been holding the pair rather than any demand for yen - today's 0.43% fall was a dollar move, with EUR/JPY down just 0.06%.

catalysts.event: OPEC+ output policy and the European gas market
catalysts.note: OPEC+ left December output targets unchanged. European gas remains the separate and worsening energy story: EU gas is 93.19 EUR/MWh and plus 26.76% on the month, German gas 98.31 and plus 32.00%, even as Brent fell 6.88% on the week. That is a euro-area growth tax the ECB named in its October statement, and it is the leg capping the DAX while Brent relief argues the other way.

geopolitics: The Strait of Hormuz has been closed long enough that the oil premium is a structural feature of this board rather than an event, and this week the premium has started to come out without the closure ending. WTI is 96.331 and plus 0.25% today, Brent 103.955 and plus 0.34%, but the week is minus 6.28% and minus 6.88% - and the physical constraint has not changed at all. What has moved is the probability traders assign to it ending, and the diplomacy underneath that probability is genuinely contradictory. On one side: Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi says Tehran's conditions are feasible if Washington demonstrates goodwill, and that Qatari mediation compressed the original seven-day proposal to two - the United States carries out a package of measures on day one, the Strait reopens and shipping returns to normal on day two. The conditions have not moved and are not small: lifting the sanctions imposed after the Islamabad memorandum collapsed in July, reinstating the oil waivers granted in June, reducing the US military presence, recognising shipping routes designated by Iran and Oman, ending the naval blockade of Iranian ports and releasing frozen funds, with Qatar working specifically on more than $6 billion in Iranian assets. Trump wrote on Truth Social that a deal could happen. On the other side: the Wall Street Journal reports the main diplomatic channel has stalled, fresh US strikes landed on the eve of the midterm elections, Iran has publicly played down hopes of ending the war, Trump paired his deal talk with a threat to bring the hammer, and the US military's position that Hormuz is open directly contradicts Tehran's. This file will not trade either narrative on its own. The FX transmission runs through four channels, and today the fourth one changed character. First, the direct terms-of-trade channel: Canada remains the clean beneficiary, USD/CAD is minus 2.10% on the month, and Macklem has now firmed the policy response, telling the Commons finance committee that further hikes may be needed and attributing the inflation pickup specifically to the Middle East energy shock rather than domestic demand. Second, the inflation channel, which is why most of these banks are tightening at all - the Fed named geopolitical developments in its October statement, the ECB warned elevated energy prices could fuel inflation while weighing on activity, the BoE attributed the rise in UK CPI directly to Middle East conflict, the RBA cited elevated fuel and commodity prices on Monday, and Switzerland today became the clearest case of all: October CPI at 1.5% against a 1.3% consensus, with energy about 96% of the net monthly increase and CPI excluding petroleum products unchanged. A genuine Hormuz reopening would pull the rug from all of those paths at once, which remains the single largest correlated risk on this board. Third, the gas channel, specific to Europe and still moving the wrong way for the euro: EU gas is 93.19 EUR/MWh and plus 26.76% on the month, German gas 98.31 and plus 32.00%, even while Brent fell 6.88% on the week - so for the euro area the energy shock is intensifying as a growth tax exactly as the oil premium deflates, and it is the leg capping the DAX. Fourth, the risk-appetite channel, which is no longer dominated by the war and today stopped being one trade. The Nasdaq 100's third correction of 2026 is a separate, disinflationary shock, and it has now visibly split: its monetary leg reversed when a Democratic Senate removed the deficit trade, so real yields fell, gold rose 1.73% back to 3999.83 and silver rose 3.01%; its demand leg did not reverse at all, with copper at its lowest since August 19 and minus 4.25% on the week. That split is the most useful fact on the board. It means the hawkish consensus here is no longer being attacked from both sides at once - but the side still under attack is the AI-demand leg that the RBA, the BoJ and the RBNZ each wrote into their own hawkish reasoning. The franc is the one currency that now has both an energy-driven inflation surprise and a haven bid that actually works, and it is the only currency that gained against all seven others today.
